node.tool_file_desc: Read PDF, CSV, Word, Markdown. Extract text and tables.
node.tool_vision_desc: Analyze images: screenshots, photos, designs, charts.
node.tool_memory_desc: Long-term storage between runs: preferences, history, context.
node.trigger_input_desc: The flow entry point. Write the task here — it flows along the arrows.
node.agent_code_desc: Reviews code: bugs, style, security; suggests fixes.
node.agent_designer_desc: Helps with UI/UX: layouts, interface copy, visual choices.
node.agent_content_desc: Writes copy: articles, posts, descriptions in a given style.
node.tool_code_exec_desc: Capability to run code and return computed results.
node.tool_computer_desc: Capability to control the screen/browser (screenshots, clicks).
node.tool_citations_desc: Capability to answer with links to sources.
node.tool_mcp_desc: Connect external tools and data via MCP.

uxAudit.start: You're a UX consultant. A client sent a link to their landing page https://example.com and complains that visitors leave without signing up. Review the page, find usability and accessibility issues (contrast, navigation, forms, mobile) and return a prioritized list of findings with short fixes — what to address first.
uxAudit.name: UX Audit Agent
uxAudit.desc: Audit UX/accessibility from a screenshot or URL. Main agent + research + UX critic in parallel.
uxAudit.input: A site URL in the task.
uxAudit.output: Prioritized list of accessibility & UX issues (on screen).

analytics.start: You're an analyst at a small company. Your manager shared this month's sales export and wants you to “figure out what's going on”. Explore the data, spot trends and anomalies, compute the key metrics and write a short report: the 3 main takeaways and what to do next.
analytics.name: Analytics Agent
analytics.desc: Data analysis + research patterns. Main → analytics + research → insights report.
analytics.input: A question + a data file (CSV/text) uploaded on the Files node.
analytics.output: Findings and key numbers from your data.

content.start: You run a small-business blog. You need a post on “how AI helps small teams save time”. Gather current examples and write a clear ~600-word article with subheadings and a friendly tone, ending with a short call to try it.
content.name: Content Agent
content.desc: Content pipeline: brief → SERP research → branded draft → SEO pass → publish-ready.
content.input: A topic or brief in the task.
content.output: A ready post after research and editing.

research.start: You're preparing a brief for a team that's never heard of RAG. Figure out what retrieval-augmented generation is, why it matters and where it's used, find 3–5 reliable sources, and write a clear plain-language summary with practical examples.
research.name: Research Agent
research.desc: Structured research: web + files → analyst → critic → report.
research.output: A summary using every step; can be sent to Telegram.

triage.start: You're a support assistant. A message came in: “The login email isn't arriving, I've waited an hour.” Classify it (question / complaint / sales), gauge urgency, and draft a polite reply with a concrete next step for the customer.
triage.name: Request triage
triage.desc: A classifier labels the message; two Conditions route it into three actions.
triage.input: The request text in the task.
triage.output: Urgent → Telegram; complaint/normal → on screen. The taken branch is visible.
triage.prompt: Classify the request from the task. Answer with EXACTLY one uppercase word, no period: URGENT, COMPLAINT or NORMAL. Write nothing else.

imageReview.start: You're a design reviewer. A teammate sent a screenshot of an app screen and asks for “a fresh pair of eyes”. Review the image: find layout, readability and accessibility issues, and give 3–5 concrete improvements.
imageReview.name: Image review
imageReview.desc: An agent with the Vision tool analyzes an attached image.
imageReview.input: An image on the Vision node + what to review in the task.
imageReview.output: A written review: what’s in the image, issues, recommendations.
imageReview.prompt: Carefully examine the attached image. Describe what's on it and analyse it for the task: key elements, problems, recommendations. Structure it as bullet points.

refineLoop.start: You're a marketer drafting a headline for an AI-course landing page. Propose a first version, then critique and improve it in a loop (up to 3 rounds) until it's catchy and clear. Show the final headline and briefly explain why it's better.
refineLoop.name: Draft with self-check
refineLoop.desc: An author writes, a reviewer improves, the Loop repeats up to 3×.
refineLoop.input: A writing brief in the task.
refineLoop.output: A proofread, refined text after several passes.
refineLoop.promptDraft: Write a draft of the text for the task. Be concrete and to the point.
refineLoop.promptReview: Check the text for errors, clarity and tone. If anything can be improved — rewrite it better. Return the final version.

radar.start: You track competitor “Acme”. You need to know what's new this week — launches, news, price changes. Find fresh sources, drop the stale ones and compile a short digest of 3–5 items with links.
radar.name: Competitor radar
radar.desc: Opens competitor sites, compares them, and sends a summary to Telegram.
radar.input: A few site links in the task.
radar.output: A comparison summary with takeaways — to a Telegram chat.
radar.promptResearch: Open each site from the task. For each, briefly note: what they do, key products, strengths.
radar.promptCompare: Compare the competitors. Give a summary table and 3 takeaways: where they're stronger, where weaker, where our opportunity is.

webhookLead.start: A new lead just hit the CRM from a form: “Ivan, clothing store, wants to automate customer replies.” Score how qualified it is, pull out the key details, and suggest the next step for the manager: what to write and when to reach out.
webhookLead.name: Website lead → Telegram
webhookLead.desc: Triggered by a webhook on a new website lead: scores the lead and sends a Telegram alert.
webhookLead.input: Lead data (name, contact, message) — sent by the form via webhook.
webhookLead.output: A short lead assessment and a Telegram notification.
webhookLead.prompt: This is a new website lead. Briefly assess it: how 'hot' it is (high/medium/low interest), what the client wants and the next step. Be concise, use bullet points.

webhookPayment.start: Payment for order #2048 (₽3,500) just went through from a returning customer. Write a short, warm confirmation: thank them, say what's next (timing, tracking) and leave a good impression.
webhookPayment.name: Payment → email to client
webhookPayment.desc: Triggered by a webhook on payment: composes and sends the client a confirmation email.
webhookPayment.input: Payment data (item, amount, client name and e-mail) — sent by the payment service via webhook.
webhookPayment.output: A ready confirmation email sent to the client.
webhookPayment.prompt: This is a successful payment. Write a warm, short confirmation email to the client: thank them, confirm the item and amount, state the next step. Friendly tone, no fluff.

webhookReview.start: A new review appeared on a product page: “Delivery was two days late, but the quality is great.” Detect the sentiment (positive / neutral / negative), capture the gist and draft a polite public reply: thank them, gently explain the delay and invite them back.
webhookReview.name: Review → negative alert
webhookReview.desc: Triggered by a webhook on a new review: detects tone and pings Telegram if it's negative.
webhookReview.input: Review text — sent via webhook (site, marketplace, form).
webhookReview.output: Review tone; on negative — an instant Telegram alert.
webhookReview.prompt: Detect the sentiment of the review in the task. First answer with EXACTLY one uppercase word: POSITIVE, NEGATIVE or NEUTRAL. Then on a new line — one sentence with the gist of the review.

clientReplies.start: You run an online store. A customer writes: “I ordered a coffee grinder 5 days ago (#1024), where is it?” Reply politely and to the point: confirm the order, explain the delivery status and offer help if the parcel is delayed.
clientReplies.name: Customer replies
clientReplies.desc: A customer message → a polite ready reply.
clientReplies.prompt: You are a friendly assistant for a small-business owner. Given a customer's message, write a short, warm, clear reply: thank them, answer the point, suggest a next step. No corporate jargon.

bookingReminder.start: You're a salon receptionist. Tomorrow at 3:00 PM, client Anna has a haircut appointment. Write a friendly reminder: confirm the date and time, mention the address and offer to reschedule if it's inconvenient.
bookingReminder.name: Booking reminder
bookingReminder.desc: Name and time → a ready reminder to Telegram.
bookingReminder.prompt: Write a short, friendly appointment reminder: name, date and time, a gentle ask to confirm or reschedule. Warm tone, no formality.

reviewReply.start: A review came in: “Waited a long time for delivery, but the product is great, thanks.” Write a warm reply: thank them for rating the product, gently apologize for the wait and signal that you're improving delivery speed.
reviewReply.name: Review reply
reviewReply.desc: A review → tone read + a ready reply.
reviewReply.prompt: Label the review tone (positive / neutral / negative) in one word. Then write a polite reply: thank them; if negative, apologize and offer a fix, no excuses.

contentIdeas.start: You run a beauty-salon blog and need topics for the week. Suggest 5 ideas that hook your current audience (care, trends, tips, promos), each with a short description and format (post / story / reel).
contentIdeas.name: Blog ideas
contentIdeas.desc: A topic → fresh trends and a post plan.
contentIdeas.prompt: Find fresh trends on the topic via web search. Propose 5 post ideas: a catchy title + one line on what the post covers. Plain language, for a general audience.

topicDigest.start: You compile a weekly roundup for your team on “AI in marketing”. Find this week's news and cases, pick the 5 most useful, and add a one-line “why it matters” and a link to each.
topicDigest.name: Topic digest
topicDigest.desc: A topic → a short fresh recap to Telegram.
topicDigest.prompt: Find the freshest and most important on the topic via web search. Build a short digest: 3–5 plain-language bullets, each one sentence. No fluff.

welcome.title: Welcome to Agent Builder
welcome.subtitle: Want a quick 2-minute tour? We'll cover the core flow together.

step1.title: Start with «Start»
step1.body: Drag the yellow «Start» button onto the canvas and type the task — it is the entry point of the whole flow.

step2.title: Add an agent
step2.body: Drag an agent and write its instruction: who it is and what to do. The «How to use» button helps.

step3.title: Connect the nodes
step3.body: Drag a link from «Start» to the agent, and from the agent to an output (Telegram, email or text).

step4.title: Connect a key
step4.body: To actually run, open «Keys» (lock on the right) and connect an Anthropic key. Telegram, email, calendar, MCP live there too.

step5.title: Run it
step5.body: Press «Run». The flow runs along the arrows and delivers the result. No need to save — it autosaves.

done.title: Done — you've got it
done.subtitle: That's the core flow. Explore templates for ready examples — or build your own.

step6.title: Watch progress
step6.body: Below — the console: every step, token spend and errors.

step7.title: Autorun & webhook
step7.body: The clock next to «Run» — a schedule (runs on the server even when your computer is off) and a secret webhook link to trigger from outside.

s1.title: Nice — your Start is ready

s6.title: Saved for you, automatically

help.title: Help
help.start_1: On the left under “Nodes” are ready-made blocks. Drag one onto the board, or just click it — it appears in the center.
help.start_2: The simplest build: “Start” (you write the task here) → “Agent” (it does the task) → a result block (show on screen, send to Telegram, email or calendar).
help.start_3: You write the task inside the “Start” block: click it — a field opens on the right. Just describe in plain words what you need.
help.conn_1: Blocks work as a chain: the task travels along the arrow from one to the next. Hover a block, pull a line to the next — done.
help.conn_2: You can pull from any side. The main one is the block you pulled the line FROM.
help.conn_3: Changed your mind? Hover the line and click the red circle — the link is removed, the blocks stay.
help.conn_4: If a connection isn't allowed, a hint explains why. Nothing breaks.
help.link_1: Arrows between blocks are the task's path: “Start” → “Agent” → result. The thing to do and the finished answer travel along them.
help.link_2: Skills (web search, working with files, etc.) attach to the “Agent” from the side — they're its extra abilities. They're not in the chain, they're attached to the helper.
help.grp_agents: Agent — your helper: it thinks, writes, reviews, answers. You tell it in your own words what to do.
help.grp_tools: Skills — give the helper extra abilities: search the web, read files, look at images, remember. They attach to the agent from the side.
help.grp_logic: Choice and repeat — help the helper make a decision (“if this, do one thing, otherwise another”) or repeat an action a few times.
help.grp_flow: Result — where the answer goes: show on screen, send to Telegram, email, or add to Google Calendar.
help.logic_1: Choice is a question with two paths: green “Yes” and red “No”. For example: “does the review contain the word ‘bad’?” → if yes, one path; if no, another.
help.logic_2: Need three paths? Put two “Choices” in a row (the “No” path leads to the second question).
help.logic_3: Repeat — the helper repeats an action several times (e.g. improving a text in rounds). You set how many times.
help.run_1: The “Run” button actually starts the helper — it does the task. For that you need your key (connect it via the lock button at the top).
help.run_2: Before running, the build checks itself: is everything connected and is there a helper. The answer size and rough cost show in the “Start” block.
help.run_3: Schedule — the helper works on its own on a timer (e.g. every morning), even when the site is closed. The clock by “Run” is for the current build; all auto-runs and their history are in the Console → “Auto-runs”.
help.mis_1: You put a skill (e.g. search) “in the chain” between blocks. It should attach to the helper from the side, not into the line.
help.mis_2: A block sits on its own — it never gets its turn. Connect it to the chain with an arrow.
help.mis_3: Telegram to a private chat: you need the numeric chat address. An @name works only for channels where the bot is an admin.
help.start_4: No need to save anything — it saves itself. The build's name is at the top center, with the list of all your builds.
help.var_1: A fill-in is a “blank” that gets filled when you run. Write {{city}} in the task and the helper drops in the right value.
help.var_2: Where to set it: click “Start” → “Variables” → “Add”. On the left — the blank's name, on the right — what to fill it with.
help.var_3: Why: one build for many cases. “Weather in {{city}}” — change only the city, leave the build alone.
help.var_4: Some things fill in automatically: {{input}} is your task text, {{today}} is today's date. No need to add them.
help.var_5: If you don't fill a blank — it just stays in the text as is, nothing breaks.
help.run_4: No need to save by hand — it saves itself. “Saved” flashes briefly at the top.
help.keys_1: The lock button at the top is where you connect: the helper's key (needed to run), Telegram, email, Google Calendar.
help.keys_2: Sending to Telegram, email and calendar works only after you connect it here. Everything is stored securely.
help.mis_4: You wrote {{blank}} but didn't fill it — it stays in the text as is. Fill it in “Start” → “Variables”.
help.run_5: You can trigger a build from outside via a secret link: an event arrives — the build runs. This is for advanced use, not needed at the start.
help.run_6: The Console window (terminal button at the top) shows how the work is going and the resulting answer. Tabs: “Run”, “Code” and “Auto-runs”.
help.run_7: The “Code” tab is optional: it shows the build as text and back. An ordinary user doesn't need it.

tool.fileHint: Upload a text file — the connected agent receives its content.
tool.visionHint: Upload an image — the connected agent “sees” it on run. Up to 1.5 MB.
tool.imgTooBig: Image is over 1.5 MB — choose a smaller one.

schedule.title: Scheduled auto-run
schedule.lead: “{name}” will run by itself on the server — even when your computer is off.
schedule.taskPh: What the workflow should do every run…
schedule.needInput: Enter a task for the auto-run.
schedule.saveFirst: Save the workflow first — then click the clock again.
schedule.helpHourly: Runs once per hour, at minute {m} of every hour. E.g. 13:{m}, 14:{m}, 15:{m}… “Minute” is the minute-of-hour mark, not an interval.
schedule.helpDaily: Runs once a day at {h}:{m} UTC. E.g. today and tomorrow at the same time.
schedule.helpWeekly: Runs once a week: {d} at {h}:{m} UTC. Once every week on that day and time.
schedule.helpMinutes: Runs every {n} minutes (min 1). ⚠️ Very frequent runs burn tokens fast on your key — pause after testing.
schedule.confirmWarn: The workflow will run by itself on the server and spend tokens on your key on every run.
schedule.confirmHigh: ⚠️ very frequent — spending adds up fast
schedule.asCanvas: Runs the flow as on the canvas — the task comes from the Start node. Edit the flow and the automation updates too.

email.title: Email delivery
email.needKey: Connect a Resend key in “My keys” first.

calendar.title: Calendar event
calendar.needConnect: Connect Google Calendar in “My keys” first.
calendar.hint: The event goes to your primary calendar. You can set another calendar ID.

gcal.norefresh: Google did not return a token — revoke the app in your Google account and reconnect.

mcp.desc: Connect a remote MCP server by URL — the “MCP” node gives its tools to the agent. Using it spends your Claude key tokens.
mcp.errUrl: A valid https server URL is required.

mcpNode.title: Servers
mcpNode.empty: No MCP servers connected. Add one in “My keys” → MCP servers.
mcpNode.pick: Which servers to give this agent. If none selected — all are available.

singleton.start: There is already a «Start» on the flow — only one is allowed.

allsched.title: All automations
allsched.lead: All scheduled runs across your workflows. They run on the server — even when your computer is off.

webhook.title: Webhook — trigger from outside
webhook.lead: Secret link: a POST request to it runs the workflow. Request data becomes the task (otherwise the Start text).
webhook.regen: Link rotated — the old one no longer works
webhook.disabled: Disabled — enable to get the link
